sentences.text: The holotype specimen of C. lyelli — the specific fossil the species is based on — measured approximately 24.5 cm in length. This animal is defined by a headshield featuring a largely tubercle-free upper surface, a tapered rostral part, a narrow dorsal median field, and lateral fields extending onto cornual horns.

Cephalaspis possessed a pair of pectoral fins and a smooth, continuous outer layer on its body exoskeleton. It was heavily armored like its immediate osteostracan ancestors, with a pineal plate fused into its headshield.
Sensory patches were located along the edge and center of its protective head shield. These patches were used to locate worms and other organisms buried in the mud.
Cephalaspis was depicted in the 2005 BBC documentary Walking with Monsters as a descendant of Haikouichthys.
Its armor likely served as a source of calcium for metabolic functions in low-calcium aquatic environments.
The type species C. lyelli was described in 1835 from Early Devonian Old Red Sandstone in Scotland. The genus Cephalaspis was named by Agassiz in 1835 as a wastebasket taxon containing four species.

Cephalaspis is thought to have been a bottom-feeder due to its mouth being situated directly beneath its head. Researchers think Cephalaspis likely fed by filtering over the sea floor because its mouth was located directly under its head.

Cephalaspis likely stirred up sand and dust with its plow-like head to sift for worms, arthropods, and detritus in the mud. It moved its head side to side like a plow to stir up sand and mud from the bottom. This behavior unearthed worms and crustaceans hidden in the mud and among algae.
Osteostracans, including Cephalaspis, likely possessed the ability to sense electrical fields.

C. lyelli, named after Sir Charles Lyell, is the type species of the genus Cephalaspis. Cephalaspis is classified as a member of the Osteostraci, recognized as close relatives to jawed vertebrates. Cephalaspis belongs to the class Osteostraci.

A 2009 study determined that Cephalaspis sensu stricto is the sister taxon of cornuate osteostracans. A 2026 study identified C. lyelli, C. fletti, and C. producta as valid members of the genus Cephalaspis. Cephalaspis belongs to the parent group Cephalaspididae.
Cephalaspis lived during the Early Devonian period. Cephalaspis lived from the Pridoli to the Emsian, between 422.7 and 393.47 million years ago.
Cephalaspis lived in freshwater streams and estuaries in western Europe during the Devonian period.

Creators of the documentary Walking with Monsters suggested that Cephalaspis or a relative was an ancestor of jawed fishes. However, Cephalaspis belongs to the class Osteostraci, which is believed to be a sister group to all jawed vertebrates.
